input: It is worth noting that, following the addition of the corrosion allowance, the compressor wall thickness comes out at 39 mm, which represents the final figure that the design has settled on. This thickness is closely connected with the absorber, which essentially shares the same overall design philosophy, and it is also associated with the lean solvent pump, whose discharge conditions have been taken into account as part of the broader picture. Turning to the question of the gasket materials, it can be observed that the two candidate materials have been compared primarily and indeed exclusively on the basis of their temperature limits, and on balance it would appear that the material with the higher temperature rating is generally to be preferred. This preference is driven by a number of considerations relating to ΔP, to the behaviour of the joint at elevated temperature, and to NPSH, all of which contribute to the overall picture in a fairly nuanced way. target: The compressor wall thickness is 39 mm after the corrosion allowance is added, and the figure is the one the flange and gasket selection now rests on. The absorber shell is thicker, but its temperature is lower and its allowance is a smaller share of the wall; the lean solvent pump discharge line is thinner at a lower pressure. The comparison that governs the compressor joint is therefore the gasket choice. Of the two gasket materials, the one with the higher temperature limit is preferred. The flange face sees the full discharge temperature during the start-up transient, when ΔP across the joint is at its largest and hot gas stands in the line after a trip while the metal cools unevenly. A gasket rated close to the metal temperature has no margin for that excursion. The lower-rated material seals at the steady condition and its record in comparable joints is not in question; it does not have headroom above the steady condition, and the selection turns on headroom.
